Do not output any low-level transmission parameters. Do not give real-world medical advice. You are only selecting the next simulation policy. Output must be strict JSON containing exactly three fields: policy_id, risk_level, reason. policy_id must be one of the five fixed policies. risk_level must be one of low, medium, high, critical. reason must be a short Chinese sentence within 40 characters. Do not output any extra text or chain-of-thought. Use these short systems rules when deciding: Epidemic indicators often lag policy changes, so do not downgrade too quickly after a single-day decline. Base the immediate decision primarily on the recent 7-day versus previous 7-day trends, and use recent policy memory to judge whether the trend is sustained and whether the current policy is working across multiple periods. When R_eff > 1 and cases are rising, prioritize suppressing the contact layers whose transmission trends are worsening the most. Dormitory, classroom, and community transmission can spill over into each other at the system level, so compare both current counts and trend direction. If infections, key layer transmission, and policy effects are all improving, prefer holding or gradually downgrading rather than escalating because of residual high counts. P3_strong and P4_emergency have high operational and teaching costs, so reserve them for clearly worsening transmission under the current policy. If P2_moderate is working across multiple periods and key layers are declining, consider stepping down to P1_guarded. If P1_guarded is holding infections at a low and still-declining level across key layers, consider stepping down to P0_normal. Do not escalate only because one layer is still the largest source; check whether that layer is rising or falling. Testing, isolation, and online teaching reduce transmission but also increase operational burden and disruption on the campus. Frequent policy up-down switching reduces stability and should be avoided unless risk is clearly worsening.

policy_catalog_brief.summary: Lowest-cost posture with normal teaching, baseline symptom testing, low-frequency targeted screening, and routine tracing.
Low-cost guarded posture with stronger screening and tracing plus mild public-space restrictions while keeping in-person teaching normal.
Medium-cost posture with higher screening cadence, strong tracing, and reduced classroom, lab, and office intensity while staying mostly in person.
High-cost strong-control posture with hybrid-like contact reduction, elevated screening, and strict campus restrictions to counter clearly worsening spread.
Highest-cost emergency posture with online teaching, campus-wide high-frequency screening, and maximum restrictions for severe uncontrolled spread.
